title: Chorionic Villus Sampling
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: CVS obtains placental tissue in early pregnancy for genetic diagnosis. It is performed 11‑14 weeks, carries a small miscarriage risk, and is valuable where later tests are unavailable.

sections.p: Chorionic villus sampling is a percutaneous procedure that retrieves chorionic villi from the placenta for cytogenetic or molecular analysis, confirming fetal chromosomal or single‑gene disorders.
b: Performed trans‑cervical or trans‑abdominal under ultrasound guidance
Indicated when a definitive prenatal diagnosis is required before 15 weeks

sections.p: The need for CVS arises from maternal or fetal risk factors that warrant early genetic information.
b: Advanced maternal age (≥35 y)
Positive first‑trimester combined screen (nuchal translucency + PAPP‑A + β‑hCG)
Family history of autosomal‑dominant or recessive disorders (e.g., sickle cell, thalassaemia)
Previous child with chromosomal abnormality

sections.p: The patient is usually an asymptomatic pregnant woman seeking diagnostic clarification. Key history points include gestational age, prior screening results, and any contraindications such as active bleeding or infection.
b: No physical signs specific to CVS; focus on obstetric assessment

t.b: Confirms gestational age (11‑14 wks) and placental location; guides needle entry
Detects aneuploidy, microdeletions, and structural rearrangements
Identifies mutations (e.g., sickle cell, thalassaemia, 21‑hydroxylase deficiency)

sections.p: Complications are rare but must be recognised promptly.
b: Miscarriage (0.5‑1 %); counsel before procedure
Placental bleeding or hematoma
Infection (chorioamnionitis) – fever, uterine tenderness
Molar pregnancy – avoid invasive sampling

sections.p: Management centres on safe performance, result interpretation, and counselling.
b: Pre‑procedure: confirm gestational age, obtain consent, screen for infection, give prophylactic oral antibiotics if local protocol advises
Procedure: sterile technique, ultrasound guidance, gentle suction of villi, limit passes to reduce trauma
Post‑procedure: observe 30‑60 min, advise rest, warn of bleeding or fever, schedule follow‑up ultrasound at 2 weeks

sections.p: After CVS, monitor for early pregnancy loss and provide genetic counselling based on results.
b: If result normal and pregnancy continues, routine antenatal care resumes
If abnormal, discuss options: continuation with specialist care, in‑utero therapy (e.g., for 21‑hydroxylase deficiency), or termination where legal
Prevent future complications by documenting any procedure‑related adverse events

sections.p: Conditions or tests that may be mistaken for CVS.
b: Amniocentesis – performed 15‑20 weeks, samples amniotic fluid, higher gestational age
Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling – invasive fetal blood draw, used for severe anemia or infections
Confined placental mosaicism – abnormal result in villi but normal fetus; may need amniocentesis for confirmation
Maternal cell contamination – can give false‑negative results; labs use short‑tandem repeat markers to detect

whenToSeekHelp: Heavy vaginal bleeding after the procedure
Severe abdominal pain or signs of peritoneal irritation

faq.q: What is the optimal gestational window for CVS?
faq.a: 11‑14 weeks; before the placenta is fully formed and before the fetal pole is easily visualised.

faq.q: How does CVS differ from amniocentesis?
faq.a: CVS samples placental tissue early (11‑14 wks) while amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid later (15‑20 wks); risk profiles and timing differ.

faq.q: Can CVS be done in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Yes, with basic ultrasound, sterile technique, and a trained operator; molecular testing may be sent to a regional lab.

exam: A 32‑year‑old at 12 weeks requests definitive testing after a high‑risk combined screen – what is the next step? — Explain indication for CVS, obtain consent, and arrange ultrasound‑guided sampling.

During CVS the operator notes a thickened placenta and difficulty obtaining villi – what should be considered? — Recognise possible molar pregnancy; stop procedure and arrange urgent obstetric review.
A patient’s CVS karyotype shows trisomy 21 but ultrasound is normal – how do you counsel? — Discuss that CVS reflects fetal genotype, explain options, and address parental concerns.
What are the main reasons CVS may give a false‑negative result? — Confined placental mosaicism and maternal cell contamination; recommend confirmatory amniocentesis if suspicion remains.

In a setting without on‑site PCR, how can a suspected sickle‑cell disease be evaluated prenatally? — Perform CVS for DNA extraction, send sample to a reference lab, or use targeted restriction‑enzyme analysis if available.

A woman develops fever and uterine tenderness 24 h after CVS – what is your immediate management? — Treat as possible chorioamnionitis: start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, monitor vitals, and arrange obstetric review.

Compare the miscarriage risk of CVS versus amniocentesis and explain why one may be preferred in early pregnancy. — CVS risk ≈0.5‑1 %; amniocentesis risk ≈0.5‑1 % but performed later; early diagnosis favours CVS when timing is critical.
Why is it important to document the number of needle passes during CVS? — Each pass increases placental trauma and loss risk; limiting passes reduces miscarriage probability.
